intro_notes: Scouts BSA Test Lab Pilot Badge (Valid through 2026-12-31). Sewing is using a needle and thread to make stitches and combine textiles by hand or machine. Needlework is decorative sewing and other textile arts. In this badge, you will investigate several types of sewing and needlework. You will learn basic hand and machine sewing skills and make several small, practical projects using your new skills!

NOTE: Any registered adult Scouting America volunteer may serve as the counselor/reviewer for a Test Lab badge. Upon completion of all requirements and the official Scouting America Test Lab survey, Scouts receive an official Certificate of Completion that converts to Merit Badge credit if the badge graduates to permanent status.

pamphlet_excerpts: Rotary Cutter Safety: Always close the blade safety shield immediately after finishing every individual fabric cut.
Needle Disposal Method: Place broken sewing machine needles inside a hard puncture resistant container before disposal.
Iron Temperature Settings: Select lower heat settings for synthetic fibers to prevent melted fabric burns.
Finger Guard Clearance: Keep hands four inches away from moving machine needles during active stitching.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Workspace Organization: Clear scissors and pins off the cutting surface before beginning fabric layout.
Step 2 - Blade Guard Check: Confirm the rotary cutter blade retracts fully into its protective safety housing.
Step 3 - Iron Station Preparation: Position the iron cord safely to avoid snagging while pressing fabric seams.
Step 4 - Machine Speed Setting: Adjust the foot pedal speed controller to low before starting any stitches.

options: A. Keep your foot on the presser-foot speed controller while reaching into the needle bar.

pamphlet_excerpts: Thimble Selection Standard: Wear a metal or leather thimble on the middle finger for control.
Thread Length Rule: Cut hand sewing thread eighteen inches long to prevent tangles and knots.
Backstitch Seam Strength: Overlapping backstitches produce durable seams that resist tension in high stress repairs.
Tailors Knot Purpose: Wrapping thread twice around the needle tip creates a neat anchored knot.
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Needle Threading: Thread the cut strand cleanly through the needle eye without fraying fibers.
Step 2 - Tailor Knot Creation: Wrap the working thread around the needle twice and pull it taut.
Step 3 - Fabric Piercing: Push the needle tip through both layers of cloth using a thimble.
Step 4 - Seam Lock Finish: Take two tiny anchor stitches in place before cutting the trailing thread.

left_points: (2a) Emergency Field Sewing Kit: A compact sewing kit contains needles, thread, small shears, safety pins, and spare buttons for field repairs. Storing these tools in a water resistant container keeps needles rust free during outdoor treks.

(2b) Needle Threading and Knotting: Threading needles smoothly requires a clean diagonal thread cut and steady finger placement. A quilter knot forms a secure ball that cannot pull through fabric weaves.

(2c) Core Hand Stitch Demonstrations: Running stitches baste temporary layers, while backstitches create permanent structural seams. Overcast stitches prevent cut fabric edges from unraveling under repeated washings.
right_points: (2d) Uniform Patch Attachment Technique: Pinning patches flat prevents fabric bunching during the application of edge stitches. A blind stitch or whipstitch around the border secures the emblem cleanly.

(2e) Button Shank Attachment Method: Sewing flat buttons over a toothpick creates necessary shank clearance for thick fabrics. Wrapping thread firmly around the raised thread stem reinforces the button against strain.

(2f) Visible Mending and Upcycling: Sashiko geometric stitching reinforces worn fabric while highlighting the mended area with decorative thread. Upcycling extends garment lifespans by turning structural damage into artistic textile embellishment.

requirements.lead_text: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement:
requirements.req_text: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement: (A) Machine Sewing (a) Provide a brief overview of the evolution of the sewing machine (b) Read your machine manual and do the following: (1) Explain the parts of a sewing machine and their functions. (2) Thread the machine and the bobbin. (3) Explain how to properly clean and oil the machine and change the needle. (c) Identify other tools you will need for machine sewing. Demonstrate the following sewing techniques, including when and why each is used: (1) Pinning (2) Sewing in a straight line (3) Back stitch (4) Basting stitch (5) Gathering stitch (6) Unpicking or seam ripping. (d) Do the following using a sewing machine: (1) Sew a Scout patch on your uniform or other fabric. (2) Repair a tear or small hole in fabric using a patch or darning technique. (e) Sew ONE item from this list using a pattern, using THREE or more techniques from requirement 3(c): (1) Drawstring backpack (2) Camp utensil holder (3) Storage bag for tent stakes or school supplies (4) Pillowcase (5) An item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor. (B) Knitting (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of knitting. (b) Explain the tools used when knitting. Demonstrate the ability to read a pattern, including deciphering symbols. (c) Using knitting needles, demonstrate how to tie a slip knot, cast on and bind off. (d) Demonstrate the following stitches: (1) Knit stitch (2) Purl stitch. (e) Knit a small item such as a dishcloth, scarf, or an item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor, using ONE of the following stitch patterns with at least two colors of yarn: (1) Garter stitch (2) Stockinette stitch (3) Ribbing. (C) Crochet (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of crochet OR the history of Amigurumi. (b) Explain the tools used when crocheting. Demonstrate the ability to read a pattern, including deciphering symbols. (c) Demonstrate how to tie a slip knot and how to hold a crochet hook and yarn to crochet. (d) Demonstrate the following stitches in a small practice piece: (1) Single crochet (2) Double crochet (3) Half-double crochet. (e) Crochet a small item such as a dishcloth, scrub, or an item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor, using at least two colors of yarn. (D) Hand Embroidery (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of hand embroidery. (b) Explain the tools used in hand embroidery. (c) Embroider a small sampler of your own design or from a purchased kit or embroider a temporary patch for your uniform. Include SIX of the following basic stitches: running stitch, back stitch, stem stitch, chain stitch, surface couching, blanket stitch, herringbone stitch, chevron stitch, feather stitch, weave stitch, seed stitch, French knots, fishbone stitch, satin stitch, cross stitch. (E) Appliqué (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of hand appliqué. (b) In a small sample, demonstrate how to do appliqué by hand using the following methods: needle turn or freezer paper using an invisible (ladder) stitch or blanket stitch. (c) (c) In a small sample, demonstrate machine appliqué using a raw edge fusible technique and a blanket stitch. (d) Appliqué a design onto a T-shirt by hand or machine or reverse appliqué a shape by hand sewing. (F) Quilting (a) Research historical quilts and show your counselor examples of types of quilts that interest you. Discuss how they were made. (b) Explain the tools used when quilting and how to use them safely. Discuss why accuracy is important in traditional quilting. Sew an accurate ¼" seam. (c) Using scraps of cotton quilting fabric, sort into light, medium and dark colors. Choose a focus fabric and find a group of fabrics that would work well in a scrap quilt. Demonstrate how the value and scale of a printed fabric can create interest. (d) Using three copies of a quilting design, color blocks to achieve different quilt designs. Show your counselor your designs and which one is your favorite. (e) Make a small quilt (12" square plus borders): (1) Using a rotary cutter, cut fabric into strips and pieces to make a four patch, rail fence block pattern, or design of your choice. Sew together on a machine or by hand using a ¼" seam allowance and press flat. Cut and add borders. (2) Make a sandwich with backing and batting. Baste. (3) Hand quilt with a running stitch or big stitch. (4) Label your quilt. Explain why this is important. (5) Bind to finish the edge of the quilt.

left_points: (3A) Mechanical Sewing Machine Operation: Modern lockstitch machines link upper needle thread with lower bobbin thread beneath the throat plate. Maintaining proper upper tension disks ensures balanced stitches that do not loop on either fabric side.

(3B) Fundamentals of Knitted Fabrics: Knitting constructs elastic textiles by interlocking yarn loops across two pointed needles using knit and purl stitches. Controlling hand tension produces uniform rows and prevents uneven fabric stretching.

(3C) Structural Crochet Stitch Practice: Crochet creates textured, sturdy textiles by pulling loops through previous stitches with a single hooked tool. Changing stitch height from single to double crochet alters fabric density and flexibility.
right_points: (3D) Surface Hand Embroidery Art: Hand embroidery decorates woven cloth using varied floss strands, specialized needles, and decorative stitch families. Hooping base fabric smoothly prevents surface distortion while stitching satin or French knot designs.

(3E) Decorative Fabric Appliqué Methods: Appliqué bonds or stitches smaller fabric motifs onto a larger background foundation to build complex pictorial designs. Securing raw edges with satin or blanket stitching prevents fraying during laundering.

(3F) Quilt Assembly and Layering: Quilting binds top patchwork, batting insulation, and backing fabric together using decorative or grid stitching lines. Basting layers securely with safety pins prevents shifting and puckering on the quilting frame.

requirements.description: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement: (A) Machine Sewing (a) Provide a brief overview of the evolution of the sewing machine (b) Read your machine manual and do the following: (1) Explain the parts of a sewing machine and their functions. (2) Thread the machine and the bobbin. (3) Explain how to properly clean and oil the machine and change the needle. (c) Identify other tools you will need for machine sewing. Demonstrate the following sewing techniques, including when and why each is used: (1) Pinning (2) Sewing in a straight line (3) Back stitch (4) Basting stitch (5) Gathering stitch (6) Unpicking or seam ripping. (d) Do the following using a sewing machine: (1) Sew a Scout patch on your uniform or other fabric. (2) Repair a tear or small hole in fabric using a patch or darning technique. (e) Sew ONE item from this list using a pattern, using THREE or more techniques from requirement 3(c): (1) Drawstring backpack (2) Camp utensil holder (3) Storage bag for tent stakes or school supplies (4) Pillowcase (5) An item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor. (B) Knitting (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of knitting. (b) Explain the tools used when knitting. Demonstrate the ability to read a pattern, including deciphering symbols. (c) Using knitting needles, demonstrate how to tie a slip knot, cast on and bind off. (d) Demonstrate the following stitches: (1) Knit stitch (2) Purl stitch. (e) Knit a small item such as a dishcloth, scarf, or an item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor, using ONE of the following stitch patterns with at least two colors of yarn: (1) Garter stitch (2) Stockinette stitch (3) Ribbing. (C) Crochet (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of crochet OR the history of Amigurumi. (b) Explain the tools used when crocheting. Demonstrate the ability to read a pattern, including deciphering symbols. (c) Demonstrate how to tie a slip knot and how to hold a crochet hook and yarn to crochet. (d) Demonstrate the following stitches in a small practice piece: (1) Single crochet (2) Double crochet (3) Half-double crochet. (e) Crochet a small item such as a dishcloth, scrub, or an item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor, using at least two colors of yarn. (D) Hand Embroidery (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of hand embroidery. (b) Explain the tools used in hand embroidery. (c) Embroider a small sampler of your own design or from a purchased kit or embroider a temporary patch for your uniform. Include SIX of the following basic stitches: running stitch, back stitch, stem stitch, chain stitch, surface couching, blanket stitch, herringbone stitch, chevron stitch, feather stitch, weave stitch, seed stitch, French knots, fishbone stitch, satin stitch, cross stitch. (E) Appliqué (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of hand appliqué. (b) In a small sample, demonstrate how to do appliqué by hand using the following methods: needle turn or freezer paper using an invisible (ladder) stitch or blanket stitch. (c) (c) In a small sample, demonstrate machine appliqué using a raw edge fusible technique and a blanket stitch. (d) Appliqué a design onto a T-shirt by hand or machine or reverse appliqué a shape by hand sewing. (F) Quilting (a) Research historical quilts and show your counselor examples of types of quilts that interest you. Discuss how they were made. (b) Explain the tools used when quilting and how to use them safely. Discuss why accuracy is important in traditional quilting. Sew an accurate ¼" seam. (c) Using scraps of cotton quilting fabric, sort into light, medium and dark colors. Choose a focus fabric and find a group of fabrics that would work well in a scrap quilt. Demonstrate how the value and scale of a printed fabric can create interest. (d) Using three copies of a quilting design, color blocks to achieve different quilt designs. Show your counselor your designs and which one is your favorite. (e) Make a small quilt (12" square plus borders): (1) Using a rotary cutter, cut fabric into strips and pieces to make a four patch, rail fence block pattern, or design of your choice. Sew together on a machine or by hand using a ¼" seam allowance and press flat. Cut and add borders. (2) Make a sandwich with backing and batting. Baste. (3) Hand quilt with a running stitch or big stitch. (4) Label your quilt. Explain why this is important. (5) Bind to finish the edge of the quilt.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While sewing a heavy canvas Merit Badge sash repair on a sewing machine, the needle hits a thick seam and snaps. What is the mandatory safety and machine procedure before replacing the needle?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While sewing a heavy canvas Merit Badge sash repair on a sewing machine, the needle hits a thick seam and snaps. What is the mandatory safety and machine procedure before replacing the needle?
options: A. Keep your foot on the presser-foot speed controller while reaching into the needle bar.
B. Turn off and unplug the sewing machine first, locate all broken needle fragments so none remain in the fabric.
C. Leave the broken needle tip inside the canvas and sew over it.
D. Hold the replacement needle between your lips while loosening the needle clamp screw with power on.
choices: A. Keep your foot on the presser-foot speed controller while reaching into the needle bar.
B. Turn off and unplug the sewing machine first, locate all broken needle fragments so none remain in the fabric.
C. Leave the broken needle tip inside the canvas and sew over it.
D. Hold the replacement needle between your lips while loosening the needle clamp screw with power on.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Turn off and unplug the sewing machine first, locate all broken needle fragments so none remain in the fabric, and insert a fresh heavy-duty needle with the flat shank side facing the correct direction.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Turning off power prevents accidental foot-pedal activation while fingers are near the needle bar, and recovering broken needle tips prevents puncture injuries.

options: A. To keep the needle from dulling against the plastic rim of the button
B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
C. To measure the exact distance between the buttonholes on the placket
D. To lock the quilter's knot on the front side of the garment
choices: A. To keep the needle from dulling against the plastic rim of the button
B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
C. To measure the exact distance between the buttonholes on the placket
D. To lock the quilter's knot on the front side of the garment
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Stitching over a pin or toothpick creates controlled slack that you wrap with thread beneath the button to form a sturdy shank, giving the buttonhole fabric space to sit flat when buttoned (p. 13).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which pair of sewing machine components works together to move the fabric forward by one stitch length after each needle penetration?
options: A. The bobbin winder spindle and the upper thread spool pin
B. The tension dial and the thread take-up lever
C. The feed dogs beneath the needle plate and the presser foot above
D. The flywheel clutch and the reverse stitch button
choices: A. The bobbin winder spindle and the upper thread spool pin
B. The tension dial and the thread take-up lever
C. The feed dogs beneath the needle plate and the presser foot above
D. The flywheel clutch and the reverse stitch button
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. The feed dogs beneath the needle plate and the presser foot above
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The toothed feed dogs rise through slots in the throat plate to grip the underside of the fabric against the downward pressure of the presser foot, advancing the material evenly between stitches (p. 16).

options: A. The warp threads, the weft threads, and the selvedge edge
B. The paper pattern, the fusible interfacing, and the outer canvas lining
C. The embroidery hoop, the monk's cloth foundation, and the yarn fringe
D. The decorative pieced top, the insulating middle batting, and the fabric backing
choices: A. The warp threads, the weft threads, and the selvedge edge
B. The paper pattern, the fusible interfacing, and the outer canvas lining

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The decorative pieced top, the insulating middle batting, and the fabric backing
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A quilt sandwich consists of three layers: the decorative top (often pieced or appliqued), the warm inner batting, and the bottom backing fabric, all joined by hand or machine quilting stitches (p. 23).
